chapters.name: Chapter 1: AI as your creative partner

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Brainstorming ideas with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to get many ideas, then pick and improve the best one.
This lesson builds toward: Given a creative project, you will use an AI assistant to list many varied ideas, then change or combine them into your own idea, getting at least five ideas and making one your own.
Brainstorming means coming up with lots of ideas fast, without judging them yet. AI assistants like ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini are good at this because they can list many ideas in seconds.
Ask for quantity and variety: "Give me 10 different ideas for a poster for our school's robotics club. Make some funny, some serious and some bold." Then you choose. The best results come when you mix AI ideas with your own.
Treat AI ideas as a starting point. Change them, combine two, or use one to spark something new. That way the final idea is truly yours.
Step by step:
- Say what you are making and who it is for.
- Ask for many ideas with different styles.
- Circle the two or three you like.
- Change or combine them into your own idea.
Words to know:
- Brainstorm: coming up with lots of ideas quickly before choosing one.
Try it now: Pick a project: a club poster, a short story, a game level or a song theme. Ask an AI assistant you are allowed to use for 10 different ideas. Pick your favorite two and write how you would change them.
You can now brainstorm with AI and turn its ideas into your own.

check.q: What is the main rule while brainstorming?
options: Come up with lots of ideas before judging them
check.why: Brainstorming means many ideas fast, without judging them yet.

check.q: AI gave you 10 poster ideas and two are close to what you want. What do you do?
options: Combine or change them and add your own spark
Ask for 100 more and never choose
check.why: Mixing AI ideas with your own makes the final idea truly yours.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Designing with free AI tools
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple poster or graphic using a free design tool.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free design tool such as Canva or Google Slides, you will make a simple poster from a template, after checking the tool's age rule and school settings, with one big title and a clear date, time and place.
Canva is a design tool with a free plan that runs in a web browser or app. Some schools also give students access through a school account, so ask your teacher. Google Slides and Microsoft PowerPoint also work for simple posters.
Start from a template (a ready-made design), then change the words, colors and pictures. Some tools can make a picture from words you type. These AI image features may have their own age rules or be turned off on school accounts, so check before you use them.
Good design is simple: one big title, a few short lines, clear colors that are easy to read, and the important facts like date, time and place.
Step by step:
- Open Canva, Google Slides or PowerPoint (use your school account if your school gives you one).
- Choose a poster template.
- Change the title, the details and the colors.
- Add or make one picture.
- Check that the date, time and place are easy to read.
Words to know:
- Template: a ready-made design you can change.
- AI image generator: a tool that makes a picture from words you type.
Try it now: Open a free design tool and pick a poster template. Put in a title and the date, time and place for your idea from Lesson 1. Save it.
You can now make a simple poster with a free design tool.

check.q: What makes a poster easy to read?
options: One big title, a few short lines and clear colors
Dark text on a dark background
check.why: Good design is simple, with a big title and the key facts easy to see.

check.q: You want to use an AI image feature in a design tool on your school account. What do you do first?
options: Make a new account without telling anyone
Check its age rule and whether your school allows it
check.why: AI image features can have their own age rules or be turned off on school accounts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Keeping your work original and giving credit
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Say honestly how AI helped and keep your own voice in the work.
This lesson builds toward: For any work where AI helped, you will write a credit note that says what AI did and what you did, and add something only you could make, following the class or contest rules on AI and using no one else's art without permission.
If AI helped you make something, say so. A short note like "Ideas brainstormed with Microsoft Copilot; design and words by me" is honest and shows you know how to use the tool.
Do not use other people's art, music, logos or characters without permission, and do not ask AI to copy a real artist's work exactly. Some schools and contests do not allow AI-made pictures at all, so read the rules.
Your voice matters. Add something only you could add: an inside joke from your club, a photo you took, a drawing, or your own words.
Step by step:
- Write down what AI did and what you did.
- Add a short credit note.
- Read the contest or class rules on AI.
- Add one thing only you could make.
Words to know:
- Credit: saying who or what helped make something.
- Copyright: the law that protects people's creative work, like art, music and writing.
Try it now: Add a one-line credit note to the poster you started. Then add one thing only you could add, such as your own photo or slogan.
You can now give honest credit for AI help and keep your own voice in your work.

check.q: Why add a credit note when AI helped?
options: It is honest and shows how you used the tool
check.why: A short credit note is honest about what AI did and what you did.

check.q: Your poster looks a lot like every other AI poster. How do you add your own voice?
options: Add your own photo, drawing, slogan or club inside joke
Ask AI to copy a famous artist exactly
check.why: Adding something only you could make keeps the work yours.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: AI as your study partner

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Learning a new skill step by step
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask AI to teach you a new skill in small steps at your level.
This lesson builds toward: Given a small skill you want to learn, you will ask an AI assistant to teach you in small steps at your level and quiz you after each one, naming the skill, your level and the one-step-at-a-time request.
AI can act like a patient tutor. Tell it what you want to learn, what you already know, and ask it to go one step at a time. For example: "I want to learn to read guitar tabs. I know nothing yet. Teach me in 5 small steps and wait for me after each one."
Ask it to check your understanding: "Ask me one question before moving on." If something is confusing, say so: "Explain that like I am 12" or "Give me an example from basketball."
Free learning sites like Khan Academy have lessons and practice you can use alongside an AI assistant. Your school may have approved tools, so ask your teacher which ones to use.
Step by step:
- Name the skill and your level.
- Ask for small steps, one at a time.
- Ask it to quiz you before moving on.
- Ask for examples from things you like.
Words to know:
- Tutor: someone (or a tool) who helps you learn one-on-one.
Try it now: Choose a small skill you want to learn this week (a chord, a math method, a drawing technique, a word in a new language). Ask an AI assistant to teach you in small steps and to quiz you after each one.
You can now use AI as a step-by-step tutor at your own level.

check.q: What should a prompt for learning a new skill include?
options: The skill, your level and a request to go one step at a time
check.why: Telling AI the skill, your level and to go step by step makes it act like a patient tutor.

check.q: The AI's explanation of a math method confuses you. What do you send?
options: "Explain that like I am 12, with an example from basketball."
check.why: Asking for simpler words or an example you like helps you understand.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making practice questions and flashcards
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your notes into practice questions and quiz yourself.
This lesson builds toward: Given your own class notes, you will create practice questions or flashcards with AI, answer them first, and check the answers, with no private information and every answer checked against your notes or textbook.
Testing yourself is one of the best ways to remember things. AI can turn your own notes into quiz questions in seconds.
Paste or type your class notes (no private information) and ask: "Make 8 practice questions from these notes. Do not show the answers until I reply." Then answer them yourself before you look.
You can also ask for flashcards: a word on one side, its meaning on the other. Free tools like Google Docs or paper cards work fine. Check the answers against your notes or textbook, because AI can still make mistakes.
Step by step:
- Collect your notes on one topic.
- Ask AI for practice questions, answers hidden.
- Answer them yourself first.
- Check the answers against your notes or textbook.
Words to know:
- Flashcard: a card with a question or word on one side and the answer on the other.
- Self-testing: quizzing yourself to help you remember.
Try it now: Take notes from one class this week. Ask AI for 5 practice questions with the answers hidden. Answer them, then check yourself against your notes.
You can now turn notes into practice questions and quiz yourself.

check.q: Why ask AI to hide the answers when it makes practice questions?
options: So the AI can grade itself
So you answer first and really test yourself
check.why: Testing yourself before seeing the answer helps you remember.

check.q: AI's answer to one practice question does not match your notes. What do you do?
options: Check your notes or textbook and trust them
check.why: AI can still make mistakes, so check against your notes or textbook.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Using AI to learn, not to skip learning
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Decide when AI help is learning and when it is skipping the work.
This lesson builds toward: Before and after you use AI for schoolwork, you will decide whether an AI use helps you learn or skips the learning, using the tomorrow test and your teacher's rules, asking your teacher first whenever you are not sure.
There is a difference between AI helping you learn and AI doing the work for you. If you ask it to explain, quiz you or give feedback, you are learning. If you ask it to write your essay or solve your homework so you can copy it, you are skipping the learning, and it may break school rules.
A good test: after using AI, could you do the task alone tomorrow? If yes, AI helped you learn. If no, try again in a way that makes you do the thinking.
Always follow your teacher's rules. If you are not sure whether something is allowed, ask before you use AI, and be ready to say how you used it.
Step by step:
- Ask AI to explain, quiz or give feedback, not to do the work.
- Check: could I do this alone tomorrow?
- Follow your teacher's AI rules.
- Be ready to say how you used AI.
Words to know:
- Feedback: comments that help you improve your own work.
Try it now: Final task: make your club or event poster. Brainstorm at least five ideas with AI, make one your own, design it in Canva or Google Slides, and add a credit note saying how AI helped.
You can now use AI for creativity and learning in a way that is honest and keeps the skill yours.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Brainstorm Fewer than five ideas, or the first AI idea was used as it was. At least five ideas, with one changed or combined into your own. Can show which ideas were combined and why that one was picked. Poster design The title or the date, time and place are missing or hard to read. One big title, a few short lines, clear colors, and the date, time and place easy to read. The design fits the club or event, and a classmate can read it from across the room. Own voice Nothing on the poster is the learner's own, or it uses someone else's art or logo. Includes one thing only the learner could add, such as a photo, drawing or slogan. Most words and choices are clearly the learner's own. Credit note No note, or it hides how AI helped. A short note says what AI did and what the learner did. The note is specific, such as which tool brainstormed the ideas. Followed the rules Used a tool or feature against its age rule, the school rules or the contest rules. Every tool and feature used is allowed for the learner's age and school. Can explain which rules they checked and where. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is using AI to learn?
options: Asking AI to explain a step you missed, then trying it yourself
Having AI solve every homework problem
Pasting AI answers into a test
check.why: Explanations, quizzes and feedback help you learn; copying skips the learning.

check.q: After AI helped, you could not do the task alone tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Try again so you do more of the thinking
check.why: The tomorrow test shows AI did the thinking, so redo it in a way that makes you learn.
